Making KV Movement Agent-Aware

Coding agents naturally pause during tool calls, then resume with tight latency expectations. Current memory movement paths are largely context-agnostic: they can move KV pages, but they do not know which agent needs them, when they are needed, or whether missing the deadline will stall replay. This project quantifies that gap and prototypes hint-guided KV movement as a path toward smarter DMA engines, KV-aware memory scheduling, and hardware/runtime co-design.

  • Core problem: memory movement sees bytes, not agent deadlines.
  • Research target: make KV movement deadline-aware and session-aware.
  • Hardware angle: smarter DMA queues, KV metadata, residency protection, and telemetry.

The testbed has controlled and real traffic

Controlled runs expose mechanisms; real traces keep the workload credible.

  • Controlled synthetic path: prompt size, tool wait, filler pressure, and replay deadline are known.
  • Real coding-agent path: SWE-bench / AgentBench traces feed DeepAgents and SGLang.
  • Both paths measure the same question: was useful KV ready before replay?

03

Today’s DMA engines move bytes, not intent

That limits how well software hints can be enforced.

  • They do not know which KV belongs to which agent session.
  • They do not know when the agent will replay after a tool call.
  • They do not know whether evicting prefetched KV wastes the hint.
  • They do not expose enough semantic telemetry: useful, late, wasted, or evicted-before-use.

Hardware opportunity: add KV/session context to the memory movement path.

The delay is not just copy time

The request passes through normal runtime scheduling before visible KV H2D begins.

Stage markers separate client submit, SGLang receive, scheduler queue/admit, H2D start, and H2D finish.

Agent-aware KV movement
09

Key findings make the hardware case

The pattern points to missing context, deadlines, residency control, and telemetry.

  • Agent tool gaps can be very short.
  • Correct hints can still finish late.
  • Visible copy time is only part of end-to-end delay.
  • KV can be written to host, evicted from GPU, then lost from host before replay.
  • Replay-side H2D movement can miss the deadline even when the replay request exists.

Conclusion: this is a scheduling and enforceability problem, not just a bandwidth problem.

Agent-aware KV movement
10

Potential hardware impact

These are ballpark research targets for tool-heavy agent workloads, not final measured claims.

  • 10-30% lower post-tool replay latency when urgent KV is ready before replay.
  • 20-50% fewer late KV reloads with deadline-aware movement scheduling.
  • Lower tail latency by prioritizing soon-resuming agent sessions.
  • Less wasted bandwidth by avoiding too-early or evicted-before-use prefetch.
  • Better effective HBM use through KV-aware residency and eviction choices.

The prototype is designed to turn these targets into measured numbers.

Agent-aware KV movement
11

Hardware support can make hints enforceable

Treat KV as deadline-sensitive memory, not generic bytes.

  • KV page/session metadata: which agent owns this KV and how urgent is it?
  • Deadline-aware migration queue: move urgent KV before less urgent traffic.
  • Residency protection: keep useful prefetched KV from being evicted too early.
  • Telemetry: count useful, late, wasted, and evicted-before-use movement.

Research question: how much replay latency and wasted movement can be avoided when KV movement has session context, priority, deadline, protection, and telemetry?
